topics.title: Reading detective: clues and feelings
topics.intro: Writers don’t always tell you how a character feels. They leave clues instead: shaking knees, a tiny wag of a tail, eyes that light up. Be a reading detective: find the clue, then say what it shows.
topics.teach: Tell your grown-up which clue helped you most to work out how a character felt, and why.
topics.talk: Ask {him} how {she} could tell that Jack was scared of the storm, even though he said he wasn’t.

topics.title: What happens next? Making predictions
topics.intro: Each story comes in two parts. After part 1, use the clues to predict what will happen. Then read part 2 and see if you were right. A good prediction is not a wild guess: it fits the clues.
topics.teach: Tell your grown-up what you predicted, which clue you used, and whether part 2 surprised you.
topics.talk: Pause a bedtime story at an exciting moment. Ask {him} what will happen next, and which clue tells {her}.

topics.title: Linking texts: a story and a fact file
topics.intro: Each story here has a true fact file about the same thing. One is made up and one is true. Read both, and look for links: what does the fact file explain about the story?
topics.teach: Tell your grown-up one fact that helped you understand a story, and how you could tell which text was made up.
topics.talk: After a story about an animal or a place, look up one real fact about it together. Did the story get it right?

topics.title: Stories with something in common
topics.intro: You have read lots of stories in this app. Here are short reminders of them, two at a time. What do they have in common, and what is different?
topics.teach: Tell your grown-up about two stories that teach the same lesson, and explain what the lesson is.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which two stories {she} knows that teach the same lesson. Can {she} think of one from a book at home?

items.prompt: How did Leo feel when he stood at the classroom door?

options.text: Nervous and shy
Cross and grumpy
options.feedback: Nothing shows he was cross. Look at his knees and his hand.

options.text: Proud and excited
options.feedback: Not yet! He held Mum’s hand so tightly that his fingers turned white.

items.explain: He gripped Mum’s hand, his knees shook, and later he stared at his shoes and went pink. He was nervous and shy.
items.passage:
First Day

Leo stood at the classroom door, holding his mum’s hand so tightly that his fingers turned white. His knees were shaking. Inside, twenty-nine children were laughing and chatting. They all seemed to know each other already.

“This is Leo,” said Miss Okafor. “He has just moved here from Scotland.”

Leo stared at his new shoes. His cheeks went pink. He did not say a word.

At playtime, Leo stood by the fence on his own. He pretended to be very interested in a crack in the wall.

Then a girl with a ponytail marched over. It was Maya. She was holding a book with a T. rex on the cover.

“Do you like dinosaurs?” she asked.

Leo looked up, and for the first time that day his eyes lit up. “Triceratops is my favourite,” he said. “It had three horns.”

“Mine too!” said Maya. “Come and sit with us at lunch. I’ll save you a seat.”

When Mum came to collect him at home time, Leo raced across the playground, waving a drawing of a Triceratops.

“Can I come back tomorrow?” he asked.

items.prompt: Who do you think ate the sausage rolls?

options.text: Biscuit the dog
Sam
options.feedback: Gran heard his ball thudding in the garden the whole time.

options.text: Grandad, in his armchair
options.feedback: He had been snoring all afternoon. Look for crumbs!

items.explain: All the clues point to Biscuit: crumbs, pastry on her whiskers, and a guilty face.
items.passage:
Who Ate the Sausage Rolls?

Gran had made a big plate of sausage rolls for Sam’s birthday party. She left them on the kitchen table to cool and went upstairs to wrap his present.

When she came back down, half the sausage rolls had gone.

“Who has been eating my sausage rolls?” she called.

Sam was out in the garden, kicking his football against the wall. Gran had heard the thud, thud, thud of the ball the whole time she was upstairs.

Grandad was asleep in his armchair, snoring loudly. He had been snoring all afternoon. His newspaper had slid onto the floor.

Biscuit the dog was lying in her basket with her nose tucked under her paw. When Gran walked in, Biscuit did not jump up to greet her as she usually did. Her ears went flat, and she would not look Gran in the eye. There were golden crumbs all over her blanket, and a flake of pastry was stuck to her whiskers.

Gran folded her arms. “Biscuit,” she said slowly, “I think you and I need to have a little talk.”

Biscuit’s tail gave one tiny, guilty wag.

items.explain: Pastry on her whiskers is evidence that she had been eating something with pastry.

items.prompt: Jack said he wasn’t scared of thunder. Was that true?

options.text: No, he was very scared
Yes, he wasn’t scared at all
options.feedback: Look at what he did: he pulled the duvet over his head and trembled.

options.text: Yes, he only came to help Ava
options.feedback: That is what he said, but Ava was fine. What did his body show?

items.explain: His actions tell the truth: he crept to Ava’s bed, squeaked and trembled.
items.passage:
Not Scared at All

“I’m not scared of thunderstorms,” said Jack at teatime. “Only babies are scared of thunder.” His little sister Ava, who was four, said nothing.

That night the storm came. Rain lashed against the windows. The wind moaned down the chimney. Then CRASH! Thunder shook the whole house.

A minute later, Jack’s bedroom door creaked open. He tiptoed across the landing, dragging his duvet behind him, and climbed into Ava’s bed.

“I’ve come to look after you,” he whispered. His voice came out as a squeak.

“I’m all right,” said Ava sleepily. “I like the noise. It sounds like giants playing skittles.”

The next flash of lightning lit up the room. Jack pulled the duvet right over his head. Ava could feel him trembling.

She patted his shoulder. “Don’t worry, Jack,” she said kindly. “I’ll look after you.”

In the morning, Mum found them both fast asleep in Ava’s little bed, with Jack’s feet sticking out of the end.

Jack never said anything about that night. But he never called anyone a baby again.

options.text: “Ava could feel him trembling.”
“It sounds like giants playing skittles.”
options.feedback: Ava said this. It shows that SHE was not scared.

options.text: “Rain lashed against the windows.”
options.feedback: This tells us about the storm, not about Jack.

items.explain: Trembling is a body clue that shows fear.

items.passage:
The Lucky Gloves

Nadia had driven in more than fifty rallies. In every single one, she had worn the same pair of old red gloves. The leather was cracked and one thumb had a hole in it, but Nadia would never race without them.

On the morning of the Mountain Rally, a young driver called Kit was sitting on the steps of his truck, staring at the ground. It was his very first rally. He kept checking his pockets, then checking them again.

“What’s the matter?” asked Nadia.

“I’ve lost my gloves,” said Kit quietly. “I can’t drive without them. The steering wheel gets too hot in the sun.” He blinked hard and looked away.

Nadia looked down at her lucky red gloves. She was quiet for a long moment.

Then she pulled them off and held them out. “Here,” she said. “They’ve always brought me luck. Maybe they’ll bring you some too.”

“But what will you wear?” asked Kit.

Nadia grinned and pulled a pair of spare gloves out of her pocket. They were brand new and very stiff. “I’ll manage,” she said.

That afternoon, Kit finished the rally in fifth place. Nadia came second, and her hands were sore and blistered. But when she saw Kit’s enormous smile at the finish line, she didn’t mind one bit.

options.feedback: This is a fact about Kit, not a clue to how he felt.

options.text: “He kept checking his pockets, then checking them again.”
options.feedback: That shows he was searching. Look for a clue about his eyes.

items.explain: Blinking hard and looking away is what people do when they are trying not to cry.

On the morning of the Mountain Rally, a young driver called Kit was sitting on the steps of his truck, staring at the ground. It was his very first rally. He kept checking his pockets, then checking them again.

“What’s the matter?” asked Nadia.

“I’ve lost my gloves,” said Kit quietly. “I can’t drive without them. The steering wheel gets too hot in the sun.” He blinked hard and looked away.

Nadia looked down at her lucky red gloves. She was quiet for a long moment.

Then she pulled them off and held them out. “Here,” she said. “They’ve always brought me luck. Maybe they’ll bring you some too.”

“But what will you wear?” asked Kit.

Nadia grinned and pulled a pair of spare gloves out of her pocket. They were brand new and very stiff. “I’ll manage,” she said.

That afternoon, Kit finished the rally in fifth place. Nadia came second, and her hands were sore and blistered. But when she saw Kit’s enormous smile at the finish line, she didn’t mind one bit.

Blaze’s Secret

Something strange was happening to Blaze.

For a whole week, he had arrived at the track yawning. On Monday he fell asleep in the garage halfway through a team talk. On Wednesday his tyres were caked in dried mud, even though it had not rained for days. And every evening, as soon as the sun went down, he said, “I’m off to bed early,” and rolled away very fast.

“Blaze is up to something,” said Turbo.

That night, Turbo followed him. Blaze did not go to bed. He drove out of the car park, through a gate and along a bumpy lane to an old, empty track in the woods. The ground under the trees was soft and muddy, and the track was full of sharp bends.

In the moonlight, Blaze practised the bends again and again. He skidded, spun round and tried again. “Come on,” he muttered. “Smooth and steady. Like Turbo.”

Turbo felt a warm glow inside his engine. He rolled quietly out of the shadows.

“Want some help?” he asked.

Blaze jumped so high that all four wheels left the ground. Then he laughed. “Don’t tell anyone,” he said. “I want to surprise them all at the next race.”

“Your secret is safe with me,” said Turbo. “Let’s start with that tricky corner.”

Squeak.

He stopped. He rolled forward again. Squeak, squeak. The noise was coming from his back left wheel.

Maya and Sam were staying with Grandma on her farm. It was March, but on Sunday morning they woke up to a world of white. Snow had fallen all night.

“Be careful when you feed the hens,” said Grandma at breakfast. “I saw a fox by the woods last week. And something keeps eating the scraps I put out for the birds.”

The children pulled on their wellies and crunched across the yard. Halfway to the hen house, Sam stopped.

“Look!” he whispered.

A line of small, neat paw prints ran across the snow. Each print had four toes, and the prints went in an almost straight line, one in front of the other. They led all the way to the old wooden shed.

On a nail by the shed door, a tuft of reddish-orange fur fluttered in the wind.

Then they heard it: a tiny rustle and a high, thin squeak. It was coming from under the floor of the shed.

Maya put her finger to her lips. Very slowly, she knelt down beside a gap at the bottom of the shed wall.

The Dragon’s Birthday (part 1)

A year ago, Sir Rowan had pulled a thorn from a dragon’s toe. Ever since then, the dragon had lived at Castle Rook. Every winter evening it lit the fires in the great hall with one fiery puff.

Lately, though, the people of the castle had been acting strangely. When the dragon came into the kitchen, the cooks quickly threw a cloth over something on the table. When it flew past the tower, the children stopped whispering and pretended to look at the clouds.

The dragon’s green head drooped. “Nobody wants me here any more,” it sighed.

Meanwhile, in the kitchen, the cook was mixing the biggest cake anyone had ever seen. Sir Rowan was hanging flags across the great hall.

“One whole year since our dragon came,” said Sir Rowan. “Has everyone remembered the candle?”

“Yes,” said the cook. “One big candle, right in the middle.” Then she frowned. “But how will a dragon blow out a candle? Every time it breathes out, it makes fire!”

Sir Rowan laughed. “We’ll find out tomorrow.”

Story: Papa’s Egg

The Antarctic winter had begun. The sun had gone, and it would not rise again for weeks. Icy winds howled across the frozen sea.

Papa Penguin stood very still. On top of his feet, tucked under a warm flap of skin, was a precious egg. Mama had laid it, then waddled away across the ice to the sea to find food.

“I’ll be back,” she had called. “Keep our egg warm!”

Papa never let the egg slip off his feet. If it rolled onto the ice, it would soon freeze.

When the storms came, Papa shuffled into the huddle with hundreds of other dads. They pressed together, beak to back, sharing their warmth. Slowly, slowly, the huddle moved round, so that every penguin had a turn in the warm middle and a turn on the freezing edge.

Week after week, Papa grew thinner and thinner.

Then one day, he felt a tap, tap, tap. A crack appeared in the egg, and out wriggled a fluffy grey chick.

At that very moment, he heard a call across the ice. He knew that voice at once. Mama was home.

Fact file: Emperor penguin dads

Emperor penguins are the biggest penguins in the world. Adults are about 1.1 to 1.2 metres tall.

Emperor penguins lay their eggs on the ice around Antarctica. The mother lays one egg as winter begins. She carefully passes it to the father, then walks to the sea to feed.

The father keeps the egg on top of his feet, under a warm fold of skin called a brood pouch. He looks after it for about two months. During all that time, he eats nothing at all.

In winter, the temperature can drop below minus 40 degrees Celsius. To survive, the fathers huddle together in groups of hundreds, or even thousands. They take turns to stand in the warm middle of the huddle.

When the chick hatches, it is covered in soft grey fluff called down. The mother comes back with food in her stomach for the chick. In the noisy crowd, she finds her family by listening for their call. Every penguin’s call is different.

Story: Papa’s Egg

The Antarctic winter had begun. The sun had gone, and it would not rise again for weeks. Icy winds howled across the frozen sea.

Papa Penguin stood very still. On top of his feet, tucked under a warm flap of skin, was a precious egg. Mama had laid it, then waddled away across the ice to the sea to find food.

“I’ll be back,” she had called. “Keep our egg warm!”

Papa never let the egg slip off his feet. If it rolled onto the ice, it would soon freeze.

When the storms came, Papa shuffled into the huddle with hundreds of other dads. They pressed together, beak to back, sharing their warmth. Slowly, slowly, the huddle moved round, so that every penguin had a turn in the warm middle and a turn on the freezing edge.

Week after week, Papa grew thinner and thinner.

Then one day, he felt a tap, tap, tap. A crack appeared in the egg, and out wriggled a fluffy grey chick.

At that very moment, he heard a call across the ice. He knew that voice at once. Mama was home.

Fact file: Emperor penguin dads

Emperor penguins are the biggest penguins in the world. Adults are about 1.1 to 1.2 metres tall.

Emperor penguins lay their eggs on the ice around Antarctica. The mother lays one egg as winter begins. She carefully passes it to the father, then walks to the sea to feed.

The father keeps the egg on top of his feet, under a warm fold of skin called a brood pouch. He looks after it for about two months. During all that time, he eats nothing at all.

In winter, the temperature can drop below minus 40 degrees Celsius. To survive, the fathers huddle together in groups of hundreds, or even thousands. They take turns to stand in the warm middle of the huddle.

When the chick hatches, it is covered in soft grey fluff called down. The mother comes back with food in her stomach for the chick. In the noisy crowd, she finds her family by listening for their call. Every penguin’s call is different.

Story: The Moving Star

Maya and Sam were camping in Grandad’s back garden. When it was properly dark, they lay on their backs outside the tent and looked up at the sky.

“Make a wish on that star,” said Sam, pointing.

“That’s not a star,” said Maya. “It’s moving.”

She was right. A bright white light was gliding smoothly across the sky. It did not flash or twinkle, and it made no sound at all.

“Is it an aeroplane?” asked Sam.

“Aeroplanes have flashing lights,” said Maya. “That doesn’t.”

Grandad came out with three mugs of hot chocolate. He looked up and smiled. “Right on time,” he said. “That’s the International Space Station. There are astronauts living up there right now. They go all the way round the Earth about every hour and a half.”

Sam waved as hard as he could. “Do you think they can see us?”

“Probably not,” laughed Grandad. “But they might be looking down at Britain all the same.”

Then the light faded away, as if someone had switched it off.

“Where did it go?” asked Sam.

“Into the Earth’s shadow,” said Grandad. “The sunlight can’t reach it now.”

Fact file: Satellites

A satellite is something that travels round and round a planet. Its path is called an orbit.

The Moon is a natural satellite. It orbits the Earth about once a month.

People have also built thousands of satellites and sent them into space on rockets. The first one, Sputnik 1, was launched in 1957. It was about the size of a beach ball.

Satellites do lots of useful jobs.
• Weather satellites take pictures of clouds and storms, so forecasters can warn us when bad weather is coming.
• Navigation satellites help a sat nav or a phone map to work out where you are.
• Some satellites send television pictures and phone calls around the world.

The biggest satellite people have ever built is the International Space Station. Astronauts live and work on board. It is about as long as a football pitch, and it travels round the Earth about 16 times every day.

On a clear night, you can sometimes see the space station from the ground. It looks like a bright star, moving steadily across the sky.

Story: Sir Rowan and the Siege

The lord of Hawk Castle had gone away, and Sir Rowan was left in charge. That was when Baron Grimwold came. One morning his army marched over the hill, with banners flying and drums beating.

“Raise the drawbridge!” shouted Sir Rowan. Chains clanked, and the great wooden bridge lifted up over the moat. Down slammed the portcullis, its iron spikes biting into the ground.

The Baron’s soldiers splashed into the moat, but the water was deep and the mud was thick. They squelched back out, dripping and grumbling.

“Then we will wait,” called the Baron. “When your food runs out, you will have to open the gates!”

So the army camped outside. Days passed. Inside, the people of the castle stayed calm. They had sacks of grain in the store rooms, and fresh water from the deep well in the courtyard. From the battlements, Sir Rowan watched the Baron’s camp.

On the seventh day, the Baron’s own food ran out. His soldiers were hungry, cold and fed up.

That evening, a delicious smell drifted over the castle walls. The cooks were baking bread.

The soldiers sniffed. Their tummies rumbled. One by one, they packed up their tents and trudged home. At last the Baron stomped off after them.

Sir Rowan lowered the drawbridge and smiled.

Fact file: Castles

After William the Conqueror won the Battle of Hastings in 1066, the Normans built hundreds of castles across England. The first ones were made of wood. Later, many were rebuilt in stone, which was much harder to burn or knock down.

A castle was a home for a lord and a fortress to keep enemies out. Here are some of the ways it did that.
• A moat was a deep ditch around the walls. It was often filled with water.
• A drawbridge could be pulled up so that nobody could cross the moat.
• A portcullis was a heavy gate made of wood and iron. It slid down to block the entrance.
• Battlements at the top of the walls had gaps for archers to shoot through, and solid parts to hide behind.
• The keep was the biggest and strongest tower. If enemies got inside the walls, people could shelter there.

Sometimes an enemy army surrounded a castle and waited, hoping that the people inside would run out of food. This was called a siege. A castle with a well and full store rooms could hold out for months.

Story: The Claw in the Rock

Noah’s Aunt Bea was a palaeontologist. In the summer holidays, she took him to a dig in a dusty, rocky valley.

“Dinosaurs walked here millions of years ago,” said Aunt Bea. She gave Noah a soft paintbrush and a little scraping tool. “Fossils break easily. Go slowly.”

All morning, Noah brushed and brushed. He found plenty of rocks. He found a beetle. He found nothing else.

Then, after lunch, his brush swept across something smooth and brown. It was curved like a hook, and longer than his hand.

“Aunt Bea!” he called. His voice wobbled.

Aunt Bea knelt beside him and gently brushed away more dust. Then she gasped. “Noah, that’s a claw. A dinosaur claw!”

It took two whole days to free the claw from the rock. The team wrapped it in strips of cloth soaked in wet plaster, just like a cast on a broken arm. When the plaster had dried hard, they lifted the claw out and packed it carefully into a box.

Months later, Noah visited the museum. There, in a glass case, was his claw, with a little card beside it:

Found by Noah, aged 7.

Fact file: Fossils

A fossil is what is left of a plant or animal that lived a very long time ago. Most fossils are found in rock.

How does a fossil form?
1. An animal dies, and its body is quickly covered by mud or sand.
2. The soft parts rot away, but hard parts like bones, teeth and shells are left.
3. More and more layers of mud pile on top. Over millions of years, they slowly turn into rock.
4. Water seeps through the rock, and minerals in it slowly turn the bones to stone.

Not only bones become fossils. Footprints, eggs and even dinosaur poo can become fossils too.

People who study fossils are called palaeontologists. They dig with brushes and small tools, because fossils can crumble. Big fossils are wrapped in a jacket of plaster to keep them safe on the journey to a museum.

One of the most famous fossil hunters was Mary Anning. She lived by the sea in Lyme Regis, in Dorset. When she was about twelve, she and her brother found the skeleton of an ichthyosaur, a sea reptile from the time of the dinosaurs.

The Crow and the Jug
A thirsty crow could not reach the water at the bottom of a jug. She dropped in pebbles, one at a time. Each pebble pushed the water a little higher, until at last she could drink. Little by little does the trick.

Two Seconds
Rosa was the newest member of the pit crew, and at first she was too slow. She practised changing her tyre again and again, until her arms ached. On race day her hands remembered everything, and the pit stop took just two seconds: the fastest of the day.

The Lion and the Mouse
A lion caught a tiny mouse, but let her go. Later, the lion was caught in a hunter’s net. The mouse heard him roaring, ran to the net and nibbled through the ropes until he was free.

The Knight and the Dragon
Everyone at Castle Rook was afraid of the dragon in the hills. Sir Rowan found it groaning in a cave and pulled a long thorn out of its toe. After that, the dragon came to live at the castle, and every winter it lit all the fires in the great hall.
